# Creating/naming objects

## Creating/naming objects

Objects can be created with either the **`<-`** or the **`=`** command

```{r, echo=TRUE}
x1 = 3 # name = object
x1

x2 <- 3 # name <- object
x2

x1 == x2 # are the two objects identical?
```

**Object names must start with a letter!! NOT "name" = ...but name = ...**

## Logical Operators

In R we can combine several relations to evaluate a given statement.

```{r,echo = TRUE}
x = 30 # Assign the value 30 to x.
```

| Function | Name                       | Example       | Result |
|----------|----------------------------|---------------|--------|
| `&`      | Conjunction (AND)          | `x>25 & x<60` | `TRUE` |
| `|`      | Inclusive disjunction (OR) | `x>25 | x>60` | `TRUE` |
| `!`      | Negation (NOT)             | `!(x<18)`     | `TRUE` |

# Vectors

## Vectors

-   **a value**: the value of the element, which can be of any type, for example a number or a string of characters

-   **a position index**: a positive integer that identifies its position within the vector.

    ![](Untitled/vettore.png)

## Creating a vector

Vectors can be created with the **`c()`** command, writing inside the brackets the values of the elements in the desired order, separated by commas.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
num_vect = c(1,2,3,4)
# you can also use the seq() function
num_vect_seq = seq(from = 1,to = 4, by = 1)

num_vect;num_vect_seq

char_vect = c("R","R","R","ok")
# you can also use the rep() function
char_vect_rep = c(rep("R", 3), "ok")

char_vect;char_vect_rep
```

## Vector type

A vector must be made of **elements all of the same type**!

```{r, echo=TRUE}
wrong = c(1,2,3,"don't know", 4)
class(wrong)
wrong
```

Otherwise you "risk" everything being converted to character.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
correct = c(1,2,3,NA, 4)
class(correct)
correct
```

## is.\* & as.\*

We can test or convert (when possible) the type of a vector with the **`is.`** & **`as.`** functions

```{r, echo = TRUE}
is.character(char_vect)
as.numeric(char_vect) #!!

is.numeric(num_vect)
as.character(num_vect) #!!

logi_vect = c(TRUE,FALSE,TRUE)
is.logical(logi_vect)

as.numeric(logi_vect)
```

## Indexing

We can select, remove and extract elements simply by using the position index inside square brackets vector\[pos\]

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Create a vector of 20 random numbers drawn between 1 and 100
my_vect = round(runif(n = 20,min = 1,max = 100))
my_vect

my_vect[1] # extract the first element

my_vect[1:5] # extract the first 5 elements

my_vect[c(1,4,2,9)] # extract elements of our choice

my_vect[length(my_vect)] # last element (why?)
```

## Negative indexing

In the same way, we can extract all the elements of the vector except some

```{r, echo=TRUE}

my_vect[-c(1)] # all except the first element

my_vect[-c(1:10)] # all except the first 10
```

## Logical Indexing

Indexing by position is the simplest and most intuitive approach. We can also select using **`TRUE`** and **`FALSE`** values: we can extract elements from the vector based on specific logical conditions

```{r, echo=TRUE}

numbers = 1:7
numbers
numbers[numbers<2]

```

# Factors

## Factors

Factors can be created either by converting a character vector with the **`as.factor()`** command or by explicitly creating a factor with the **`factor()`** command

```{r, echo=TRUE}

char_vect = rep(c("hello","ciao", "hola"), each = 2)
my_fact = as.factor(char_vect)

my_fact2 = factor(rep(c("hello","ciao", "hola"), each = 2))

my_fact == my_fact2
```

## Properties of factors

In practice, they assign a label to an integer value:

```{r, echo = TRUE}
typeof(my_fact)
```

```{r, echo=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
as.integer(my_fact)
my_fact
```

## Factor levels

Factors store **`levels()`** as metadata, regardless of which ones are actually present in the vector

```{r, echo = TRUE}
levels(my_fact)

my_fact2 = my_fact[my_fact!="ciao"]
my_fact2
```

However, we can drop the levels that are no longer needed with the **`droplevels()`** command

```{r, echo = TRUE}
droplevels(my_fact2)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also rename the levels of a factor

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# the factor I created
my_fact

# create another factor "my_fact_lev" identical to "my_fact"
my_fact_lev = my_fact
my_fact_lev == my_fact

# rename the levels of the factor
levels(my_fact_lev) = c("italian","english","spanish")

my_fact_lev

my_fact

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can both reorder and rename the levels of a factor with the **`factor()`** function

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_fact
# by default levels are assigned in alphabetical order
as.integer(my_fact)

new_fact = factor(my_fact, levels = c("hello","ciao","hola"))
new_fact
as.integer(new_fact)

new_fact2 = factor(my_fact, levels = c("hello","ciao","hola"),
                   labels = c("english","italian","spanish"))
new_fact2
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Remember**: the ***`levels`*** argument inside the **`factor()`** function is used to **reorder** the levels of the factor, while the **`levels()`** function **renames** them, it does not reorder them!

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# the factor I created
my_fact
as.integer(my_fact)
levels(my_fact) = c("hello","ciao","hola")

# What do you notice compared to the my_fact vector shown above?
my_fact
as.integer(my_fact)
```

# Lists

## Lists

Lists are flexible structures that can contain objects of different types and different sizes (each element can itself be a list)

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_list = list("hello!", 1:3, c(TRUE,FALSE),
               list("hello!", 1:3, c(TRUE,FALSE)))
str(my_list)
```

## Lists

Although a list is one-dimensional, it develops in depth

```{r, echo=TRUE}
str(my_list)
```

## Lists

***First Level***: list

```{r, echo=TRUE}
str(my_list[2])
```

***Second Level***: numeric vector

```{r, echo=TRUE}
str(my_list[[2]])
```

***Third Level***: integer

```{r, echo=TRUE}
str(my_list[[2]][1]) # integer
```

## Lists

We can assign names to the elements of a list...

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_list_nam = list(word = "hello!",numbers =  1:3,
                   logical = c(TRUE,FALSE),
               list = list("hello!", 1:3, c(TRUE,FALSE)))
my_list_nam
```

## Lists

... and access them by calling them by "name" with the **`$`** operator

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_list_nam$word

my_list_nam$list # list created as an element of the list
```

## Lists - Attributes

Like vectors, lists also have a length (**`length()`**) and possibly names (**`names()`**). The **`str()`** (structure) command is very useful for lists because it gives an overview of their structure:

```{r, echo=TRUE}

length(my_list_nam); names(my_list_nam)

str(my_list_nam)
```

## Lists - Indexing

The difference between the square brackets is whether we want to subset the list, getting another list, or directly access the inner element:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_list_nam[1] # getting another list

my_list_nam[[1]] # accessing the inner element
```

## Lists - Indexing

If we want to select several elements (i.e. actually subset the list) we must always use single square brackets:

```{r, echo=TRUE}

# list made of the first two elements of my_list_nam
my_list_nam[1:2]
```

## Lists - Nested Indexing

Lists have a one-dimensional structure that can develop in depth. To select nested elements we can chain several brackets:

```{r, echo=TRUE}

my_list_nam[[4]]

my_list_nam[[4]][[1]]

my_list_nam[[4]][[2]]

```

# Matrices

## Matrices

Matrices are a **two-dimensional** data structure (characterized by 2 dimensions, **`dim()`**), where the number of rows is dimension 1 and the number of columns is dimension 2.

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_mat = matrix(data = 1:10, nrow = 2, ncol = 5, byrow = FALSE)
my_mat
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
matrix(data = 1:10, nrow = 2, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
```

## Matrices - Properties

-   They can contain **only one type** of data

-   Since they are **two-dimensional**, we need two position indices (rows and columns) to identify an element

-   They can be seen as a **set** of single **vectors**

## Matrices - Properties

The number of rows and columns does not have to be the same (square matrix), but the size of the matrix must be compatible with the data vector:

```{r, echo=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
matrix(data = 1:10, ncol = 3, nrow = 3)
```

## Matrices

What does R do by default?

```{r, echo=TRUE, warning=FALSE}

matrix(data = 1:10, ncol = 3, nrow = 3)

matrix(data = 1:2, ncol = 3, nrow = 3)

```

**`warnings`**: the function informs us about something potentially problematic, but (more or less!!) everything is fine

## Matrices - Indexing

To identify one or more elements of a matrix we need row and/or column indices separated by a comma, again inside square brackets: matrix\[row, column\]

```{r, echo=TRUE}

my_mat
my_mat[1,1]

```

## Matrices - Indexing

We can also select an entire row or column

```{r, echo=TRUE}

my_mat[1,]

my_mat[,1]

```

## Matrices - Indexing

As with vectors, here too we can apply logical indexing:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_mat>2

# All the elements greater than two
my_mat[my_mat>2]

```

## Vectors and Matrices

Vectors are created with the **`c()`** function and can be concatenated using the same function:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
my_vect1 = c(1:4); my_vect2 = c(5:10)
my_vect12 = c(my_vect1,my_vect2)
my_vect12
```

## Matrices

Similarly, matrices can be joined together with the **`cbind()`** and **`rbind()`** commands:

```{r, echo=TRUE}

my_mat = matrix(1:4,2,2)

cbind(my_mat, my_mat)

rbind(my_mat, my_mat)

```

# Dataframe

## Dataframe

The dataframe is the most "complex", useful and powerful structure in R. Intuitively it is an excel sheet, while from R's point of view it is a type of list with some properties/restrictions

-   each element of the list is a **vector** with an **associated name** (aka a column)
-   each list/column must have the same number of elements
-   as a consequence, each row has the same number of elements (**rectangular structure**)

## Creating a dataframe

With the data.frame() function we can create a dataframe...

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Create a dataframe with 3 columns
my_df = data.frame( col1 = 1:4, col2 = letters[1:4],
                    col3 = rnorm(4))
my_df
```

## Attributes

The **`dataframe`** has both the attributes of a **list**, i.e. the ***names***, and the attributes of a **matrix**, i.e. the ***dimensions*** (rows and columns)

```{r, echo=TRUE}
typeof(my_df)
attributes(my_df)
dim(my_df)
```

## Indexing

We can use either square brackets **`[]`** or the dollar sign **`$`**

```{r, echo = TRUE}
my_df[1] # extract a 4x1 data.frame
my_df[[1]]# extract the first column of the data.frame
my_df$col1# extract the first column of the data.frame
my_df[1,1]# extract the first element of the first column of the data.frame
```

## Indexing - Relational operators

One of the most common operations you will deal with is extracting/evaluating a subset of the values in your dataset:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# keep only the rows where the values of column1 are greater than 2
my_df[my_df$col1 > 2, ]
my_df[my_df[1] > 2, ]
```

## Examples

```{r}
my_df
```

::: incremental
-   `my_df[my_df$col1 > 1 & my_df$col1 < 4, ]`
    -   2 b -0.5630882
    -   3 c -0.5672335
-   `my_df[my_df$col1== 1,  "col3"]`
    -   -1.481937
-   `my_df[my_df$col1== 1,  3]`
    -   -1.481937
:::

## Indexing

There are also alternative, more compact ways of indexing. For example, using the **`subset()`** function:

```{r,echo=TRUE}

subset(iris, subset = Species == "setosa" & Petal.Length > 1.7)

```

equivalent to:

```{r,echo=TRUE}

iris[iris$Species == "setosa" & iris$Petal.Length > 1.7,]

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also select columns rather than rows with the ***`select`*** argument:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
head(subset(iris, select = c(Sepal.Length, Species)), n = 3)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also combine the two:

```{r,echo=TRUE}
head(subset(iris, Species == "setosa" & Sepal.Length > 4,
             c(Sepal.Length, Species)), n = 3)
```

equivalent to:

```{r,echo=TRUE}

head(iris[iris$Species == "setosa" & iris$Sepal.Length > 4,
          c("Sepal.Length","Species")],n = 3)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## \$\$\$\$\$\$

Most of the time you will access variables with the **`$`** operator. This command can also be used to create a new variable...

```{r,echo=TRUE}
iris$sum = iris$Sepal.Length + iris$Sepal.Width
str(iris)
```
